notes: Complete EWHC Ch judgment on VAT liability for fast-food sales through self-employed van operators.

enrichment.short_title: VAT tribunal wrongly treated Mr Sizzle van operators as agents rather than principals under purchasing contracts
key_facts: Ringside Refreshments supplied raw food and loaned vans and kiosks to self-employed operators under written purchasing contracts; operators cooked and sold fast food to the public under the Mr Sizzle brand.
The VAT and Duties Tribunal found a single catering business and held Ringside liable for VAT on retail sales, but disallowed a penalty.
Ringside appealed on a point of law, arguing the tribunal erred by treating operators as agents and misapplying the Burrell substance-and-reality test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court from the VAT and Duties Tribunal on a point of law under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision on agency reversed.
enrichment.ratio: Where self-employed operators are not employees and purchasing contracts on their face provide only for a principal-to-principal sale of ingredients followed by resale to the public, the correct starting point is contractual construction; a tribunal errs in law if it treats extensive operational control as determinative of agency without reconciling that conclusion with the contract terms and without finding the agreements were shams or were operated inconsistently with them.
legal_issues: Whether operators selling cooked food to the public were making supplies as principals or as agents for Ringside
Whether the tribunal applied the wrong legal test by relying on Burrell and operational control rather than contractual terms
Whether the Kieran Mullin Ltd approach to self-employed stylists applied by analogy

notes: Complete EWHC Ch judgment refusing zero-rating for SITA airline telecommunications network services.

enrichment.short_title: SITA airline telecommunications network not zero-rated under Article 15.9 or Schedule 8 item 10
key_facts: SITA, a Belgian non-profit cooperative, maintained a telecommunications network used by airline members for reservations, baggage handling, maintenance and related messages, but not flight operations.
Customs and Excise withdrew a long-standing zero-rating ruling from 1 July 1997; the VAT and Duties Tribunal rejected SITA's exemption claims in January 2003.
SITA contended its network services met the direct needs of aircraft under Article 15.9 and amounted to making arrangements for passenger transport under Schedule 8 item 10.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court from the VAT and Duties Tribunal against refusal of zero-rating.
enrichment.ratio: A telecommunications network that merely processes messages initiated by airline members is too remote from aircraft operation to meet the direct needs of aircraft under Article 15.9, which must be construed strictly; likewise, providing a communications facility is not the making of arrangements for passenger transport within Schedule 8 item 10 merely because members use it in their transport businesses.
legal_issues: Whether SITA's network services met the direct needs of aircraft under Article 15.9 of the Sixth Directive
Whether SITA was making arrangements for passenger transport under Schedule 8 Group 8 item 10
Whether CSMA on making arrangements for credit was applicable by analogy

notes: Complete EWHC Admin s 288 planning challenge by Romany gypsy claimant against Green Belt refusal.

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy caravan site appeal quashed for failure to address temporary planning permission
key_facts: Romany gypsy claimant sought planning permission for a family caravan site at Sauleskalns, Sutton-at-Hone, Kent, in the Green Belt without prior consent.
Inspector Fieldhouse recommended dismissal; the First Secretary of State agreed, finding inappropriate Green Belt development without very special circumstances.
Claimant challenged weight given to emerging policy H22, personal need assessment, and failure to consider temporary planning permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash the Secretary of State's planning appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application succeeded on third ground only; decision quashed for reconsideration of temporary permission and proportionality.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant expressly requested temporary planning permission to seek an alternative site if permanent permission were refused, the Secretary of State must address that issue expressly; a general human-rights proportionality paragraph dealing only with outright refusal does not suffice to dispose of the temporary-permission question.
legal_issues: Whether adequate reasons were given for attaching considerable weight to emerging policy H22
Whether personal need for a gypsy site was distinguished from personal hardship under Hedges
Whether the Secretary of State failed to consider temporary planning permission and Article 8 proportionality in relation to it

notes: Complete EWCA Civ negligence appeal concerning reversing over intoxicated pedestrian.

enrichment.short_title: Driver liable for failing to use nearside mirror when reversing over collapsed drunk pedestrian
key_facts: Michelle Bannister reversed her father's car about 35 yards down a residential cul-de-sac at night and ran over Frank Green, who had collapsed drunk in the road.
Recorder Goose found she was not negligent in choosing to reverse but failed to keep adequate lookout by not using mirrors or looking over her left shoulder; liability apportioned 40:60 against her.
Green suffered tetraparesis and remains wheelchair-bound; Bannister briefly drove forward in panic, dragging him further.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against finding of negligence and, alternatively, contributory negligence apportionment following county court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; negligence and causation findings upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A driver who elects to reverse a substantial distance down a constricted, ill-lit street at night must exercise a high degree of care including checking nearside mirrors; failure to do so is negligent and causative where, on the evidence, the pedestrian would probably have been seen in time to stop.
legal_issues: Whether reversing down the cul-de-sac without using mirrors breached the standard of care of a reasonably prudent motorist
Whether failure to use mirrors was causative of the accident
Whether encountering an inert drunk pedestrian was outside reasonable contemplation under Glasgow Corporation v Muir

notes: Complete EWHC Ch judgment on Class 1 NIC liability for post-employment restrictive covenant payments.

enrichment.short_title: Class 1 NIC payable on £2.2m restrictive covenant payments to former director after employment ended

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: RCI Europe paid £2.2 million to former director Julian Haylock under a December 1994 severance agreement for post-termination restrictive covenants, after his employment ended on 31 July 1994.
The Special Commissioner held the payments chargeable under section 313 ICTA 1988 and therefore earnings under section 4(4) of the 1992 Act.
RCI argued section 313 required connection with employment status rather than termination, and section 4(4) required payment during active employment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court on a question of law from a Special Commissioner's decision under section 56A of the Taxes Management Act 1970.
enrichment.ratio: Payments for restrictive undertakings given in connection with past office-holding, including in a termination agreement, fall within section 313 ICTA 1988; section 4(4) treats such sums as earnings from the relevant employment relationship even when paid after employment ends, and employed earner refers to the status to which the payment is attributed rather than current gainful employment.
legal_issues: Whether post-termination restrictive covenant payments were chargeable under section 313 ICTA 1988
Whether section 4(4) required the recipient to be gainfully employed at the date of payment
Whether Regulation 6A of the 1979 Regulations fixed the earnings period

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory analysis with clear conclusions on both section 313 and section 4(4) issues.

notes: Complete EWHC Ch liability trial on Thames passenger boat operators' joint tender breach.

enrichment.short_title: Thames boat operators breached joint tender agreement and held licence on constructive trust
key_facts: Thames Cruises and George Wheeler Launches operated Westminster-Greenwich passenger services jointly through WPSA and agreed to submit a combined tender when LRS introduced competitive licensing.
Wheeler secretly met LRS, formed a rival consortium excluding Thames Cruises, and won the pier licence in December 2001.
Thames Cruises claimed partnership breach, implied duty of good faith, and Pallant v Morgan constructive trust over the licence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial on liability only following competitive tender for Thames pier licence.
enrichment.outcome: Partnership and implied good-faith claims failed; constructive trust claim succeeded on breach of joint-bid understanding.
enrichment.ratio: WPSA was a coordinating association rather than a partnership at law; absent fiduciary duties, parties who agree to pursue a joint tender cannot secretly compete and retain the resulting licence for themselves when the understanding was to bid together and the departure destroyed the agreed strategy without giving the co-bidder a fair opportunity to address concerns.
legal_issues: Whether WPSA constituted a partnership under the Partnership Act 1890
Whether implied terms of good faith precluded competing bids
Whether breach of joint-tender understanding gave rise to a Pallant v Morgan constructive trust over the licence

notes: Complete EWHC Fam Hague Convention return application concerning Portuguese children.

enrichment.short_title: Father's pretended consent to children staying in England did not amount to Hague acquiescence

statutes_considered.title: Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980

key_facts: Portuguese father Jose A applied for return of children F (13) and I (9), who had lived with him for four years and came to England for summer holiday contact with mother Precinda A in August 2003.
Mother contended father acquiesced in late August when he agreed by telephone they could remain and said he would send their clothes.
Father said he pretended to consent fearing mother would hide the children; he initiated Hague proceedings in early October 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Hague Convention summary return proceedings in the Family Division.
enrichment.outcome: Return to Portugal ordered; acquiescence defence rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Acquiescence under Article 13 depends on the wronged parent's actual subjective intention; a parent who pretends to consent to retain children at a known address does not acquiesce if he acts without unreasonable delay to secure their return once it is clear they will not go back voluntarily.
legal_issues: Whether the father's late-August consent constituted acquiescence under Article 13(a)
Whether pretended consent can negate acquiescence where the parent promptly seeks return
Exercise of discretion if acquiescence were established

confidence.notes: Complete judgment applying established acquiescence principles to pretended consent facts.

notes: Complete EWCA Civ paired appeals on Consumer Credit Act exemption for credit hire agreements.

enrichment.short_title: Credit hire deferred-payment agreements exempt where payment required within twelve-month period
key_facts: Alpha and Western credit hire companies provided replacement vehicles to accident victims with deferred payment until third-party claims concluded or up to twelve months.
County court judges held the Alpha and Western agreements exempt from CCA regulation because payments were required within twelve months beginning with the agreement date.
Appellants argued Ketley required payment before period expiry, so agreements permitting payment at expiry were regulated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal from county court decisions on CCA exemption in credit hire test cases.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; agreements held exempt.
enrichment.ratio: Where a credit hire agreement defers payment for a period not exceeding twelve months from the start of the agreement and requires payment when that deferral period ends, the obligation arises within the prescribed twelve-month period and satisfies Article 3(1)(a)(i) of the 1989 Order; Ketley turned on different wording requiring payment on expiry after twelve months.
legal_issues: Whether twelve-month deferral periods beginning with the agreement date include the agreement date
Whether payment due at the end of the deferral period is required within the exempt period
Effect of Ketley v Gilbert on differently worded credit hire agreements

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment with detailed contractual and regulatory construction.

notes: Complete EWCA Civ appeal on implied contract for architectural fees in Tangiers development projects.

enrichment.short_title: Architect entitled to implied payment from GMH from September 1994 for Tangiers project work
key_facts: Architect Dinkha Latchin produced extensive designs from 1994 for hotel, tennis club and villa projects in Tangiers for businessman Nadhmi Auchi and GMH group companies.
Recorder Uff found no express contract but implied obligation to pay reasonable fees from 1 September 1994 after work intensified with instructions to submit designs to authorities.
Auchi initially treated work as speculative; Latchin hoped to be appointed architect if projects proceeded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from preliminary issues in the Technology and Construction Court on existence and terms of contract.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed save that personal contract with Auchi on projects 2, 1 and 3 set aside; GMH liable; project 4 personal contract upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An implied contract for professional fees arises by necessity where a client gives and the architect carries out substantial instructed work at the client's request after an initial unpaid speculative phase, unless expressly stipulated otherwise; the normal commercial inference from instructions and performance is a duty to pay, rebuttable only for a limited initial period.
legal_issues: Whether an implied contract arose from parties' conduct after initial unpaid speculative work
Whether implication satisfied the Baird Textiles necessity test for intention to create legal relations
Whether GMH or Auchi personally was the contractual counterparty for each project

notes: Complete EWCA Crim appeal on cannabis possession conviction and sentence with PII issues.

enrichment.short_title: Cannabis import conviction safe despite cut-throat defences; sentence reduced to three years
key_facts: Anthony Walton was stopped on the M20 in July 2001 with 15kg of cannabis resin in his jeep after O'Callaghan placed two bags in the vehicle in West Kilburn.
Walton and co-defendants ran cut-throat defences blaming each other; Walton claimed he was set up by O'Callaghan, whom he did not name until trial.
PII material was withheld; trial judge refused independent counsel at PII hearing and gave linked-defendant directions during summing up.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with leave against conviction and, alternatively, sentence following Crown Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeal allowed in part (four years reduced to three years).
enrichment.ratio: A trial judge is not required to appoint independent counsel at a PII hearing where defence interests can otherwise be protected; comments that guilt of one co-defendant may support another's case are not misdirections where standard separate-consideration directions are given and defences stand or fall together on the evidence; a four-year sentence for 15kg Class B cannabis with intent to supply was excessive.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge should have appointed independent counsel at the PII hearing
Whether summing-up comments linked co-defendants' guilt impermissibly
Whether failure to name O'Callaghan early was misdirected in a cut-throat defence
Whether four years' imprisonment was manifestly excessive and disparate
